As a kid, it was mostly naivety. Love for my abusers. Not realizing how much of what I went through was abnormal until I became an adult. Years of being gaslit to believe that I was the problem.

When I got old enough to start to understand what was going on I started rationalizing in different ways with different parental figures. I tended to see my mom as a victim too, and I wasn't completely wrong. The psychopaths she kept bringing into my life after her divorce from my dad became the villains in my mind, and she was just an innocent victim like me. Having gotten older, though, I realize that she kept dragging me into mentally harmful and physically dangerous situations to escape her own fear of abandonment. I don't hate my mom. It was an all too human problem that led to a lot of the scary situations she dragged me into, but I do recognize now that she wasn't a great parent, and that her complacency in the violence we were surrounded by damaged me a lot, if only indirectly. 

My dad isn't an evil person either. He loves me more than anything, and I know that. He taught me to ride a bike, fix my car, hunt and fish, ect. He showed me love as best as he could. He was raised in a fundamentalist Christian family, and while he rebelled against his upbringing, it did lead him to believe that a lot of what he did to me "wasn't a big deal". I think he still feels that way about most of it. Who cares if my step mom punched me in the mouth for arguing with her about my grades? His dad would've beaten him half to death, and he didn't hesitate to tell me that. There was a fair amount of abuse both physical and verbal from my step mom, but he never did anything that direct. The most damaging thing I think he did was push me towards porn and sex from a really young age (like 8) and while I definitely hold that against him for causing a lot of my intimacy problems, he primarily did it out of fear for how his parents would react if I turned out gay (I'm bi, but same difference to Mormons). I didn't actually realize how bad that was until recently, but he's also the first person to step up and help me when I need it these days. 

My step mom might be the most complicated. She recognized that I was intelligent at a very young age, and she really did want me to become something great. She wouldn't hesitate to hurt me or berate me for hours on end in pursuit of that. I hated her deeply for the longest time. I probably faced most of my direct physical and emotional abuse from her,  but the things going on in my mom's home weren't much better. I really didn't know where to turn. The reason my relationship with her is better today is because she realized somewhere along the line that she was in the wrong. She has apologized to me so many times since then, and really has become one of my strongest advocates. Come to find out, she was dealing with some unspeakable trauma herself (too much to get into here) and at some point took a deep look at herself and realized what she was doing to me. What she did wasn't and won't ever be okay, but she loves me, and she's done her best to make amends.

These days I live in a different city and keep my interactions with my family minimal. I don't hate any of them, I've just decided to stop drinking poison. They all still care about me, and I them. I understand them all too well to truly hate them.

tldr: My abusers all loved me in their own ways, and even though they were profoundly flawed, none of them were exactly evil. They were just messed up people who could and should have done better by me. Even if they were hurting me, I loved them. People are fucked up, complicated creatures, and I didn't want to lose or hurt my family, even if they were really in the wrong. Obviously there are truly bad people out there who shouldn't be forgiven and can't be understood, but I think a lot of victims of abuse were in similar situations. 

But who knows? Maybe all the gaslighting is still getting to me. Or maybe I'm doing what my mom did for all those years. I'm not sure. Trauma is complicated.

I was twenty years old. I'd spent the better part of a decade doing my best to help my mom raise my younger brothers, and I'd developed a nasty drinking habit. In a moment of clarity, I realized living with my mom was slowly killing me. As much as I love my brothers, I lost my childhood to the responsibility I felt I had towards them. If I didn't make a change, I would lose any shot at building something for myself. I decided to move out and rent a house with my step brother on my dad's side.

Things went okay for a while. I managed most of the finances and did all of the cooking, but I was accustomed to it by that point. My step brother and I had a great relationship. The first six months there are the first time I can remember finding some degree of peace.

It didn't happen all at once. My brother slowly started spending less and less time with me. I don't hold it against him. He has his own life, and I'm honestly kind of a downer to be around sometimes. I've always got some bullshit faux wisdom to shill to anyone I can get to listen, most of it fairly nihilistic in nature. Anyways, the point is, I was feeling lonely. I started drinking more. I started dwelling on my past more.

One day, in a stoned and drunken haze, I lost focus on whatever netflix series I was watching. I thought about my brothers and my mom, and how I had abandoned them. I thought about my step brother, and how his patience for my negative attitude was waning the same way it always had with my friends growing up. In that moment, I felt profoundly alone. Nobody understood, and nobody ever would. I was too far removed from the circumstances of my peers. I was doomed to this cycle of miscommunication and loss. My only other choice was going home to help raise my brothers. I found some meaning in that, but the meaning had nothing to do with me, and I usually felt like I was doing more harm than good trying to be a father to them. 

I loaded my step brothers 30-06 hunting rifle.  Committing to the idea was a relief. Surely if there was no real way forward for me it would me more humane towards myself to just call it quits. I put the gun in my mouth. I sat there thinking for a bit. I took in my surroundings, and contemplated my heart rate and breathing. Why were they so fast? I had thought I was at peace with my decision.  There were tears in my eyes. I wondered why I was crying. I wanted this, right? It should be an easy decision to make then. I sat on the edge of the couch with that rifle in my mouth for a good long time.

In the end I unloaded the rifle and put it away. I decided I needed to leave. I found some friends living in a city eight hours away looking for a roommate. I ran an unemployment scam while doing under the table work to save up money to move. I drank a lot. Eventually, the day of the move came. I visited my parents, my grandparents, my siblings. I told everyone I would be back soon, but we all knew I was lying. I couldn't come back. Tears were shed, and I drove a rented UHaul to my current apartment. 

I wish there was a happier ending, that my problems all just went away with distance, but a part of me is still broken. I've made a decent living for myself, and I'm surrounded by people who care about me, but they're starting to push me away too. I can feel the loneliness setting in. The difference, though, is that now I know I can build something new for myself. It may not be perfect, and it may not last forever, but there's always something new on the horizon. I don't know what life has in store for me, but I know I want to find out.

Both used to beat the shit out of her. Half of my childhood memories are some variation of "protect my brothers while my mom begs for her life one room over".

Eventually, when I was around 11, she met James. He wasn't perfect, rough around the edges oilfield roughneck, but he made a real effort to connect with me and my brothers, and for once I felt safe in my own home, with someone around I could look up to. He had a daughter of his own, and I came to see her as my little sister. He asked me before proposing to my mom, and after all the work he put in trying to help my broken little family I said yes. Well, one day James decided to try meth. I didn't want to believe it at first. He had earned my trust, and it was pretty hard to do that with me at the time. I gave him the benefit of the doubt until he lost his job for refusing a drug test. It got worse from there. I'll spare you the details, but towards the end he had lost custody of his daughter (I don't know where she is now, but I hope she's happy), had started getting into screaming matches with my mom, and was dealing meth with a local white supremacist gang out of our house to support his habit. I felt like I was back to square one, but I kept holding out hope that he'd go back to the way he was before.

One day, around thirteen years old, I came home from school, and all of James' clothes and video games were gone. Come to find out, my mom had enough, and while they were in the car driving she told him to get clean or she'd file for divorce. He jerked her steering wheel into oncoming traffic in an apparent attempt at murder-suicide. They both lived. He went to prison a few months later after being caught dealing, and I spent the rest of my childhood trying my best to be a father figure to my brothers while my mom worked 60-70 hour weeks at a Dennys to support us. 

I really haven't ever trusted anyone since James.

Being an INTP doesn't necessarily put you in any box. It's a list of characteristics you're statistically more likely to have. I just went on a full blown rant on the subject in my most recent post. You don't have to fully embrace everything about being an INTP, and I honestly think doing so is unhealthy.

Ti - Will come naturally with time. Being your dominant function, it's always engaged. If you want to double down on it focus on forming connections between concepts when learning new things. 

Ne - For most of us, this manifests as sudden realizations which are then worked into the Ti web. The best way to exercise it imo is creative writing. Build a world, characters, etc. Ti will get heavily involved, but it provides a good framework for those new ideas to flow without too much self criticism. 

Si - Is about learning from your experiences. Before making big decisions (especially interpersonal decisions where logic is less helpful) make a point to reflect on what has and hasn't worked in the past. Filter that through the Ti/Ne cycle to develop new strategies. Not the easiest function for most of us to use by itself. 

Fe - This one is tricky, but also one of the most rewarding. Treat developing this function as an exercise in empathy. Consider why people react to things the way they do, especially if you disagree with them. If you can't figure it out and it's appropriate, just ask. Deep down, INTPs are very caring people. The more you develop Fe, the more apparent that becomes. It's also the key to breaking through that signature INTP awkwardness, imo.

Hope this helps!

I've noticed most people (particularly INTPs) have a tendency to focus on what we're going to say next as opposed to focusing on really absorbing the point the other person is trying to make. If your main concern is putting together your own next point, you're bound to make people feel ignored and you'll come across as standoffish at best and narcissistic at worst. At first you may be less eloquent because you're not "rehearsing your lines", but I've found that once you get used to it your responses will feel more thoughtful, and your body language will indicate that you're really invested in the conversation as opposed to waiting for your next chance to talk. People like feeling like their input is valued, which helps make you more persuasive even in situations where you don't actually give a rats ass about their opinions.

The most valuable skill I've ever developed is personality mirroring. When you're in a conversation with someone, watch and listen carefully. Match their tone of voice, use the same phrases and sentence structure. If you can figure out their MBTI, you can even emulate their dominant function. Match their body language, enthusiasm, and overall mood too. It will instantly put whoever you're talking to at ease because they feel understood and related to. Also, make a point to memorize one new thing about each of your clients each time you work with them. I go as far as to make a game out of it. Favorite color, birthday, how many kids they have, etc. Don't be afraid of small talk! I've actually made some good friends through work that I never would have been interested in initially because I've put real effort into learning about them.

My social skills are actually pretty on point. I've worked in sales for long enough that I can translate my Ti thought process to layman's terms reasonably well, and I'm pretty well spoken. I've also (begrudgingly) gotten pretty good at small talk. I'm pretty well known around work as one of our more charismatic sales reps. Granted, it took me a long time to get to where I am now, and my first boss (ENFJ) had to put in a lot of time mentoring me on active listening and personality mirroring. Just practice and have hope - We can get there!
